etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English kyn, from Old English cynn (“kind, sort, rank”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuni, from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“race, generation, descent”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁yom, from *ǵenh₁- (“to produce”).

Cognate with Scots kin (“relatives, kinfolk”), North Frisian kinn, kenn (“gender, race, family, kinship”), Dutch kunne (“gender, sex”), Middle Low German kunne (“gender, sex, race, family, lineage”), Danish køn (“gender, sex”), Swedish kön (“gender, sex”), Icelandic kyn (“gender”), Finnish kunnia (“honour, glory”), Ingrian kunnia (“reputation”), and through Indo-European, with Latin genus (“kind, sort, ancestry, birth”), Ancient Greek γένος (génos, “kind, race”), Sanskrit जनस् (jánas, “kind, race”), Albanian dhen (“(herd of) small cattle”).

definitions.definition: (collectively) Persons of the same race or family; kindred.

quote.citation: c. 1620, Francis Bacon, letter of advice to Sir George Villiers
quote.text: You are of kin, and so must be a friend to their persons.

quote.citation: 2014, Elizabeth Kolbert, The Sixth Extinction: An Unnatural History, Picador, →ISBN, page 84:
quote.text: Based on the number of teeth ammonites had—nine—it's believed that their closest living kin are octopuses.

definitions.definition: One or more relatives, such as siblings or cousins, taken collectively.

quote.citation: 2016, Saraswati Raju, Santosh Jatrana, Women Workers in Urban India, page 280:
quote.text: Among those who derive information related to work from personal contacts, nonkins, rather than kins, constitute the most important sources even for women.

definitions.definition: Relationship; same-bloodedness or affinity; near connection or alliance, as of those having common descent.

quote.citation: 1814 May 9, [Jane Austen], chapter XIII, in Mansfield Park: […], volume III, London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC, page 248:
quote.text: Such sensations, however, were too near a kin to resentment to be long guiding Fanny's soliloquies.

definitions.definition: Related by blood or marriage, akin. Generally used in "kin to".

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Mandarin 琴 (qín), from a non-palatal dialect akin to Peking; or less likely, from Japanese 琴 (kin).

definitions.definition: Alternative form of qin (“Chinese string instrument”)

quote.citation: 1899, Hugo Riemann, Catechism of Musical History: History of musical instruments and history of tone-systems and notation:
quote.text: Originally they had only two cither-like instruments, which had flat sound-boxes without fingerboards, over which were strung rather a large number (25) of strings of twisted silk — the kin and tsche.

quote.citation: 1840, Elijah Coleman Bridgman, Samuel Wells Williams, The Chinese Repository, page 40:
quote.text: If a musician were going to give a lecture upon the mathematical part of his art, he would find a very elegant substitute for the monochord in the Chinese kin.

definitions.definition: (transitive, fandom slang) To identify with; as in spiritually connect to a fictional or non-fictional being.
(fandom slang) A fictional or non-fictional being whom one spiritually connects to. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
(fandom slang, in the form (character name) kin) Someone who identifies with a certain fictional character.

quote.citation: 1959 January 5, Walt Kelly, Pogo, comic strip, →ISBN, page 4:
quote.text: [Owl:] Oh I ain't stealin' this dime... I just took it for safe-keepin'.  [Turtle:] Ain't much you kin do with it—'cept make a phone call.
